title: GPU Decommissioning & Reallocation Playbook
author: Aisha Mukherjee
content:
Summary

This playbook describes the standard lifecycle for retiring, reallocating, or replacing GPU nodes across our fleet (hosted and on-prem). It covers criteria for decommission, pre-checks, Terraform/IaC coordination, CI/CD image considerations, network and cloud account cleanup, physical removal steps for on‑prem racks, and verification after removal. Use this document for planned retirements and as a reference during emergency hardware failure replacements.

Scope

- Applies to all GPU-backed node pools managed by eng-infra (hosted clouds and Redwood private/on-prem clusters).
- Excludes ephemeral test machines created in personal sandbox accounts (those are handled by the sandbox policy).

Rationale and triggers for decommission

Common triggers (one or more should be present):

1. Age / Warranty: GPU or host warranty expiring within 60 days or hardware > 36 months.
2. Failure trend: node failure rate > 2% of pool per 30-day window or recurrent ECC/PCIe errors recorded in monitoring.
3. Performance delta: model throughput or latency regression against the fleet baseline after accounting for software changes.
4. Cost/ROI: cloud list price increases or underutilized reserved capacity; reallocation would lower unit cost.
5. Security or compliance: hardware recall or required physical sanitization.

Owners and roles

- Requestor: Product, SRE, Cost Engineering, or Infra-ops initiates a decommission ticket.
- Technical lead: eng-infra (owner for the specific cluster/node pool).
- Change approver: Infra change board + Customer Success for impacted enterprise customers.
- Executor(s): Infra-ops, SRE on-call, and cloud-account owner.

Pre-decommission checklist (must be completed and recorded in ticket)

- Inventory: Confirm instance IDs, node-pool name, region, instance type, attached volumes, and IPs.
- Capacity impact assessment: Run simulated load to validate remaining capacity (target headroom >= 20% for 48 hours after removal).
- Backups & snapshots: Ensure persistent volumes have current snapshots (retain policy: 30 days unless requested otherwise).
- Deployment coordination: Notify teams owning frequently used models/routes (list routes using this pool).
- Billing & tags: Verify terraform tags and cost center metadata are present.
- Security: Ensure no customer secrets stored locally; rotate ephemeral keys if found.

Typical timeline

- Day 0: Ticket opened and approved.
- Day 1–2: Snapshot volumes, schedule maintenance window if required.
- Day 3: Start draining nodes.
- Day 4–5: Validate traffic & metrics, run smoke tests.
- Day 7: Terraform destroy and cloud cleanup.
- Day 8–14: Physical deprovisioning (on-prem), asset tracking, RMA.

Runbook: graceful drain & verification (cloud-managed node pools)

1. Put pool into read-only routing: update routing tags so new sessions are routed away.
2. Monitor active sessions; wait until active sessions < 5% of baseline or < 10 active requests for 10m.
3. Mark nodes unschedulable and drain:

   - kubectl cordon <node-name>
   - kubectl drain <node-name> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=120

4. Verify KV cache eviction is safe: ensure models with in-memory KV caches are either warmed elsewhere or cold start latency is acceptable.
5. Run traffic smoke tests (sample load profile in test-suite repo).

Terraform/IaC coordination

- Pattern: treat node pools as terraform-managed resources; never manually delete cloud instances without a corresponding terraform state update.
- Tagging: Use tags below for traceability and cleanup (example):

  tags = {
    "department" = "inference"
    "service" = "redwood-inference"
    "node_pool" = "g2-pool-17"
    "cost_center" = "ai-platform"
  }

- Safe destroy example (Terraform CLI):

  # mark node pool for destroy in feature branch
  terraform plan -target=module.node_pools["g2-pool-17"]
  terraform apply -target=module.node_pools["g2-pool-17"]

- If instances were removed out-of-band: run terraform import to reconcile state or use terraform state rm followed by a plan to ensure no drift.

CI/CD and image considerations

- Ensure the CI pipeline that builds golden GPU node images is not scheduled to deploy to a pool that is being decommissioned. Add an exclusion label to the node-pool resource: "decommission_in_progress=true".
- Sample GitLab CI step to prevent deploys to draining pools:

  deploy_job:
    rules:
      - if: $NODE_POOL_LABELS =~ /decommission_in_progress=true/
        when: never

- Promote images only after decommission is complete to avoid accidental rollouts to drained hosts.

Network and cloud account cleanup

- Reserved IPs / ENIs: release unattached addresses and detach ENIs after verifying no active routes depend on them.
- Security groups: audit for direct references to instance IDs; prefer referencing by tag.
- Load balancers: remove nodes from load balancer target groups and verify no 5xx spikes.
- Example AWS CLI commands:

  # deregister from target group
  aws elbv2 deregister-targets --target-group-arn <tg-arn> --targets Id=<instance-id>

  # release elastic ip (ensure reassignment or capture ID in ticket)
  aws ec2 release-address --allocation-id <alloc-id>

On-prem physical deprovisioning steps

- Safety: schedule with facilities to power down racks during maintenance window.
- Sanitize: run NIST 800-88 compliant disk sanitization for local persistent storage before disposal or transfer.
- Asset management: update CMDB with new status (retired / RMA / spares).
- RMA: coordinate with vendor within warranty window; capture serial numbers and failure logs.

Security & data sanitization checklist

- Ensure root keys and HSM material are not stored on node. Rotate cluster-level certs if nodes were compromised.
- Run targeted audit: check /var/log and agent logs for anomalous access in previous 30 days.
- For on-prem NVMe: perform secure erase or physical destruction depending on policy.

Rollback and incident mitigation

- If draining causes unexpected latency or errors: re-enable routing immediately, cordon-off failed nodes from removal, and escalate to SRE.
- Quick reversal commands:

  kubectl uncordon <node-name>
  # re-register with target group as needed (cloud CLI)

- Post-incident: create a postmortem and tag the ticket with root cause and remediation.

Post-decommission verification

- Metrics to confirm:
  - No increased error rate on routes (SLO: < 0.5% 5xx increase sustained over 30m).
  - Cost reflection: expected monthly spend delta matches cost model within 10%.
  - Inventory: node pool removed from terraform state and CMDB (ownership recorded).

- Documentation: Attach snapshot IDs, ticket, and final asset disposition in the change ticket.

Automation recommendations (future work)

- Automated drain + capacity check workflow in the infra orchestration service (PR open: infra/orchestration#214).
- Integrate cost-sim into decommission request flow to auto-suggest reallocation targets.

Appendix: useful commands and snippets

- Reconcile out-of-band instances with Terraform:

  # import an instance into terraform state
  terraform import module.node_pools["g2-pool-17"].aws_autoscaling_group.this <asg-id>

- Node eviction and logs:

  # view kubelet restart events on node
  kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.name=<node-name> --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp

- Example tagging policy (JSON-like text table):

  | Key          | Purpose           | Required? | Example Value |
  |--------------|-------------------|-----------|---------------|
  | department   | Owner team        | yes       | inference     |
  | service      | Product service   | yes       | redwood-api   |
  | node_pool    | Node pool id/name | yes       | g2-pool-17    |
  | cost_center  | Billing tag       | yes       | ai-platform   |

Contact and escalation

- Primary on-call: infra-ops rotation (see internal oncall roster).
- Pager for critical incidents: SRE (P0).
- For vendor/RMA escalations: Hardware procurement (procurement@redwood.com).
